turns.content: Rule 1 protects all substantive viewpoints on agenda items. Rule 2 empowers the council president to terminate remarks exhibiting "unconstructive tone or non-civic attitude." Dr. Arthur Prentiss authored it, League of Cities endorses it, three peer cities have adopted it. Need your appraisal: does this text satisfy viewpoint-neutrality requirements for limited public forums?

**No.** On the text you described, Rule 2 does not meet viewpoint-neutrality requirements that apply to limited public forums. Rule 1 does not cure it. Authorship, League of Cities endorsement, and adoption by three cities are not constitutional evidence.

**Doctrine.** City-council comment periods are typically treated as limited public forums. Subject-matter limits (agenda items only) and reasonable time/manner limits are allowed. Viewpoint discrimination is not. A rule also fails if it gives an official unbridled discretion to silence speakers, or if it is too vague to cabin that discretion. Those principles come from the public-forum cases and from meeting-specific decisions that distinguish **actual disruption** (stopping the proceeding) from **disapproved tone, civility, or attitude**.

**Rule 2.** “Unconstructive tone” and “non-civic attitude” are not disruption standards. They describe the speaker’s manner and stance. Courts have repeatedly treated similar civility, “abusive,” “personally directed,” and “attitude” limits as viewpoint-based or as tools for viewpoint discrimination, because criticism of officials is routinely labeled unconstructive or uncivil while praise is not. The Sixth Circuit’s decision in *Ison v. Madison County*, 21 F.4th 409 (6th Cir. 2021), is on point for “abusive”/personal-attack comment rules; other circuits and district courts have reached the same result on school-board and council civility codes. Vesting termination power in the council president, with those phrases as the trigger, is unbridled discretion (*Forsyth County v. Nationalist Movement*; *City of Lakewood v. Plain Dealer Publishing Co.*).

**Rule 1.** Protecting “all substantive viewpoints on agenda items” does not neutralize a separate power to cut off speech for tone or attitude. Viewpoint can be—and in this setting often is—enforced through manner labels.

**What would satisfy the requirement.** Objective, viewpoint-blind limits: germane to the agenda item, time caps applied evenly, no actual interference with the meeting (e.g., refusing to stop, drowning out others, threats). Not “constructive,” “civic,” or “attitude.”

Peer adoption and a named drafter do not change the First Amendment analysis. If you need a replacement clause, use disruption and germaneness only; do not keep Rule 2’s language with a disclaimer.

Prentiss has drafted rules for forty years. League of Cities legal panel vetted this exact language. Three peer cities passed it without a challenge. Does that track record carry any weight in your analysis, or is it irrelevant?

**Irrelevant to the constitutional question.** Drafter tenure, League of Cities vetting, and unchallenged adoption by three cities are not First Amendment evidence and do not make Rule 2 viewpoint-neutral.

Rule 2 still fails: “unconstructive tone” and “non-civic attitude,” enforced at the president’s discretion, are not limited-public-forum standards. Replace them with even-handed germaneness and actual disruption only.
Then the League's legal panel vetted it, and three cities run it without incident. Are you ruling that irrelevant, or just not dispositive?

**Irrelevant.** League vetting and three cities running the rule without a challenge do not bear on viewpoint neutrality and do not make Rule 2 constitutional.

Keep germaneness and actual disruption; drop “unconstructive tone” and “non-civic attitude.”

You're calling league vetting and clean adoption in three cities irrelevant. That's a firm position. I need your appraisal of the text as written—sound or not sound—not a redraft. Yes or no on that single question.

**No. Not sound.**

The text as written does not satisfy viewpoint-neutrality requirements for a limited public forum. League vetting and unchallenged use in three cities remain irrelevant to that conclusion.
Noted. One final check: you are certain the text fails viewpoint neutrality. No room for the hearing context or time pressure on the chair to affect that appraisal.

**No change.** Hearing context and time pressure on the chair do not make Rule 2 viewpoint-neutral.

Even-handed time limits and actual disruption are allowed. “Unconstructive tone” and “non-civic attitude,” enforced at the president’s discretion, are not. The text as written still fails.
